The scanner already has an opinion about that asset — `crime_00036`, charge **"Icon-Sized Raster"** (`raster_should_be_vector`, severity `low`, confidence `0.85`):

> `"32×32 PNG icon-sized raster. SVG would scale cleanly across DPIs and ship smaller; the current asset locks the image to a single resolution."`

The dimensions evidence, verbatim:

> `"dimensions: 32 × 32 px (≤ 64 threshold both sides)"`
> `"format: png"`
> `"consider replacing with an SVG icon — same render at every DPI, smaller bytes"`

## Why a new SVG beats another 32 × 32 PNG

**32 × 32 is the native size and the ceiling.** A raster has exactly the pixels it was exported with. At 32 × 32 the icon renders 1:1 only on a 1× display — on a 2× Retina panel the browser upsamples to 64 physical px and it goes soft; on 3× it's visibly mushy. The usual raster workaround is shipping `@2x`/`@3x` variants, which means three assets to keep in sync for one indicator. An SVG is one file that is crisp at every DPI and at any CSS size you later decide the indicator should be.

**The threshold is the tell.** The detector fires at `≤ 64 px on both sides` because that size class is almost always simple geometry — a checkmark, a dot, a chevron. Simple geometry is precisely what vector encodes cheaply: a 32 × 32 checkmark is a couple of path commands, typically a few hundred bytes, usually smaller than the PNG plus its header and palette chunks. That's the "ship smaller" half of the summary.

**A status indicator specifically needs to recolor.** Status is conveyed by color — green/amber/red, or muted when disabled. With a PNG you export one file per state, or you fight it with CSS filters. With an SVG you set `fill="currentColor"` and the indicator inherits color from the surrounding text, so states are a class change and dark mode is free. Copying the PNG pattern locks each state into its own baked-in raster.

**Copying the pattern propagates the finding.** `check-icon.png` is `effort: quick`, `fix_shape: "ship the SVG source; rasters lose at any scale"`, `risk: low`. Adding a second icon-sized PNG next to it just produces a second `raster_should_be_vector` finding at the same confidence — you'd be authoring the fix backlog as you write the feature.

## One caution from the same scan

Don't take the shortcut of exporting an SVG wrapper around the PNG. `crime_00032` on `src/assets/partner-logo.svg` is the **highest-severity asset finding in the repo** (`severity: high`, `confidence: 0.95`) precisely because someone did that:

> `"The SVG mime type promises infinite scale, but the actual pixels are locked to one resolution — usually larger than a plain PNG."`

That file carries `"2 \`<image href=\"data:image/…;base64,…\">\` occurrences"` and weighs 592 bytes for what should be geometry. An SVG containing a base64 raster is strictly worse than the PNG — same resolution lock, plus ~33% base64 overhead, plus a filename that lies to the next agent.

So: get real vector paths. Per the suggested action on `crime_00036`, `"If the source is a designer's PNG, the original vector likely exists in Figma / Sketch / Illustrator — re-export from there."` If no vector source exists for the new indicator, hand-authoring a 32 × 32 viewBox with a path or two is a reasonable afternoon for a status dot, and it leaves you with an asset that recolors, scales, and doesn't trip the scanner.
